turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. In you come. Bit of a wait, I'm afraid, the list overran.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh I don't mind. Parking was a nightmare, mind you. I very nearly went home, it's nothing really.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She always says that. I'm her husband, I do the looking-after. I wasn't having her skip it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. What have you come about, then?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): When I roll over in bed the room goes round for a second or two. Same if I look up to the cupboard. I lie still and it stops. I've overdone it in the garden, that's all.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): The room spins on turning in bed. How long has that been happening?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, last week, Tuesday I think, well actually maybe the Sunday, no, stick with last week. It's nothing.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's not last week, love. Week before last it started, nearer three weeks. I'm in the bed next to her and I hear her gasp and grab the duvet.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not grab the duvet, and it is a week. I just wait and it stops. You're making a meal of it.

[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'll say you put it at about a week, and your husband puts it nearer three weeks. Both on the note. Does it come on when you're just sitting still, or only with those movements?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Only if I turn or look up. Sat still I'm fine. Of. Hardly worth all this.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sick with it at all?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit queasy. Afterwards I feel like a wet rag, then it passes. Nothing to write home about.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yesterday morning she was sick. Breakfast came straight back up. I cleaned the bowl.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not sick. Felt a bit green, sat on the bed, nothing came up. He's wrong.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. Nausea from you, and a disagreement about actual vomiting. Any ear pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Ears don't hurt.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your hearing, any loss, or any ringing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No hearing loss. I can hear his telly perfectly, too perfectly. I can't hear myself think in that front room.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The news isn't loud.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the telly. Any headache, double vision, weakness in an arm or a leg, or slurred speech?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. My feet feel dead when I first stand up, cold lino, that's all, ignore it.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dead meaning numb? Both feet, and does it ease?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Both of them. Once I'm pottering it's gone. Oh, and a frog in my throat, croaky, and I can't tell you when that started, few days I suppose.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Croak for a few days, start date unclear. Pain in the throat, or trouble swallowing?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just the croak. It's nothing.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets taken for the spinning?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): For the spinning, out-of-hours gave me stematil, five milligrams. I took one tablet and stopped it, knocked me for six. Never took another.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There was talk of an antibiotic as well, and one of those sickness patches. She never collected the antibiotic. The patch was never actually given.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): So that's prochlorperazine, five milligrams by mouth, a single dose, then stopped. I won't list the antibiotic or the patch, you never had them. What do you take every day?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine. Five milligrams, every morning, for the blood pressure. That's it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise. Brief spinning on turning in bed or looking up, for seconds, with nausea, a croak and morning numb feet, and no ear pain, hearing loss, headache or weakness. Duration somewhere between a week and three weeks. One dose of prochlorperazine then stopped, and amlodipine five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. Still feels like a lot of fuss.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 72 beats a minute, blood pressure 136 over 84. I'd like to do a Dix-Hallpike test now, head turned to the right, then I'll lie you back. You may spin for a moment.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. Two seconds of daftness.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. There's a brief rotatory flicker of the eyes on the right, gone in about fifteen seconds. Sit up when you're ready.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh. That's the one. Ridiculous, isn't it.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I'm seeing fits benign positional vertigo. Crystals shifting in the right ear canal, that's the working impression. It doesn't look like a stroke from the story or this test.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Crystals. Charming.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No new tablet from me. I'll teach you the Brandt-Daroff exercise. Sit on the edge of the bed, turn your head one way, lie onto that side until the spinning stops, sit up, then the other side, three times a day. Don't drive in the middle of a spin.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll see she does them. She'll tell you she won't bother.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight anyway, booked with me, so we can check it. If the spinning turns constant, or there's a sudden bad headache, weakness, or slurred speech, don't wait for that appointment, go to A&E the same day.

spec.situation: Spinning for a few seconds when turning in bed or looking up, since last week; nausea; no hearing loss, no ear pain; doctor does a positional test and teaches the exercise.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

omissions.text: Ringing in the ears/tinnitus was specifically asked about and denied.
Prochlorperazine 5 mg was stopped after one dose because it 'knocked me for six' (sedating/intolerable side effect).
Dix-Hallpike was performed with the head turned to the right before lying back.
The right-sided rotatory eye movements/nystagmus lasted about 15 seconds.
Doctor stated it does not look like a stroke based on the history and examination/test.
Brandt-Daroff exercise instructions were described: sit on the edge of the bed, turn the head one way, lie onto that side until the spinning stops, sit up, then do the other side.
Follow-up was specified as 'booked with me' in a fortnight.
